claim: Drosophila olfactory projection neurons (PNs) are the second-order olfactory neurons that receive organized input from olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) at approximately 50 stereotyped and individually identifiable glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: PNs are the second-order olfactory neurons that receive organized input from olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) at ~50 stereotyped and individually identifiable glomeruli in the antennal lobe, and carry olfactory information to higher brain centers (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Wilson, 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Wilson, 2013) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: PNs carry olfactory information to higher brain centers.
source: PNs are the second-order olfactory neurons that receive organized input from olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) at ~50 stereotyped and individually identifiable glomeruli in the antennal lobe, and carry olfactory information to higher brain centers (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Wilson, 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007; Wilson, 2013) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Different types of PNs send their dendrites to a single glomerulus or multiple glomeruli.
source: Different types of PNs send their dendrites to a single glomerulus or multiple glomeruli (Marin et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2012; Bates et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Marin et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2012; Bates et al., 2020).

claim: PNs are derived from three separate neuroblast lineages—anterodorsal, lateral, and ventral lineages, corresponding to their cell bodies' positions relative to the antennal lobe.
source: PNs are derived from three separate neuroblast lineages—anterodorsal, lateral, and ventral lineages, corresponding to their cell bodies' positions relative to the antennal lobe (Jefferis et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Jefferis et al., 2001).

claim: PNs produced from the anterodorsal and lateral lineages (adPNs and lPNs) are cholinergic excitatory neurons.
source: PNs produced from the anterodorsal and lateral lineages (adPNs and lPNs) are cholinergic excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: The fate of uniglomerular excitatory PN types, defined by their glomerular targets, is predetermined by their lineage and birth order.
source: The fate of uniglomerular excitatory PN types, defined by their glomerular targets, is predetermined by their lineage and birth order (Jefferis et al., 2001; Marin et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Jefferis et al., 2001; Marin et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012).

claim: PNs produced from the ventral lineage (vPNs) are GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: PNs produced from the ventral lineage (vPNs), on the other hand, are GABAergic inhibitory neurons (Jefferis et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Jefferis et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2013; Parnas et al., 2013).

claim: The connectivity and physiology of PNs have been systematically studied.
source: The connectivity and physiology of PNs have also been systematically studied (Bhandawat et al., 2007; Jeanne et al., 2018; Bates et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Bhandawat et al., 2007; Jeanne et al., 2018; Bates et al., 2020).

claim: The study obtained single-cell transcriptomes of Drosophila olfactory projection neurons (PNs) at four developmental stages.
source: Here, we obtained the single-cell transcriptomes of Drosophila olfactory projection neurons (PNs) at four developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and describes the main experimental approach of the study.

claim: The study decoded the identity of 21 transcriptomic clusters corresponding to 20 PN types.
source: We decoded the identity of 21 transcriptomic clusters corresponding to 20 PN types and developed methods to match transcriptomic clusters representing the same PN type across development.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and describes a key finding of the study.

claim: The study developed methods to match transcriptomic clusters representing the same PN type across development.
source: We decoded the identity of 21 transcriptomic clusters corresponding to 20 PN types and developed methods to match transcriptomic clusters representing the same PN type across development.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and describes a methodological contribution of the study.

claim: PN transcriptomes reflect neurite growth and pruning during metamorphosis at an early pupal stage.
source: We discovered that PN transcriptomes reflect unique biological processes unfolding at each stage—neurite growth and pruning during metamorphosis at an early pupal stage; peaked transcriptomic diversity during olfactory circuit assembly at mid-pupal stages; and neuronal signaling in adults.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PN transcriptomes show peaked transcriptomic diversity during olfactory circuit assembly at mid-pupal stages.
source: We discovered that PN transcriptomes reflect unique biological processes unfolding at each stage—neurite growth and pruning during metamorphosis at an early pupal stage; peaked transcriptomic diversity during olfactory circuit assembly at mid-pupal stages; and neuronal signaling in adults.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PN transcriptomes reflect neuronal signaling in adults.
source: We discovered that PN transcriptomes reflect unique biological processes unfolding at each stage—neurite growth and pruning during metamorphosis at an early pupal stage; peaked transcriptomic diversity during olfactory circuit assembly at mid-pupal stages; and neuronal signaling in adults.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At early developmental stages, PN types with adjacent birth order share similar transcriptomes.
source: At early developmental stages, PN types with adjacent birth order share similar transcriptomes.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eighteen out of 40 types of adPNs are born embryonically and participate in the larval olfactory system.
source: Eighteen out of 40 types of adPNs are born embryonically and participate in the larval olfactory system.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: During the larval stage, the rest of adPNs and all lPNs are born.
source: Then, during the larval stage, the rest of adPNs and all lPNs are born (Jefferis et al., 2001; Marin et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Jefferis et al., 2001; Marin et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012).

claim: During early metamorphosis following puparium formation, embryonically born PNs first prune terminal branches of dendrites and axons.
source: During early metamorphosis following puparium formation, embryonically born PNs first prune terminal branches of dendrites and axons, and then re-extend their dendrites into the future adult antennal lobe, and axons into the mushroom body and lateral horn following the neurites of larval-born PNs (Marin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Marin et al., 2005).

claim: Embryonically born PNs re-extend their dendrites into the future adult antennal lobe, and axons into the mushroom body and lateral horn following the neurites of larval-born PNs.
source: During early metamorphosis following puparium formation, embryonically born PNs first prune terminal branches of dendrites and axons, and then re-extend their dendrites into the future adult antennal lobe, and axons into the mushroom body and lateral horn following the neurites of larval-born PNs (Marin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Marin et al., 2005).

claim: From 0 to 24 hr after puparium formation (APF), PNs extend their dendrites into the developing antennal lobe and occupy restricted regions.
source: From 0 to 24 hr after puparium formation (APF), PNs extend their dendrites into the developing antennal lobe and occupy restricted regions.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: ORN axons begin to invade antennal lobe at approximately 24 hr APF.
source: ORN axons begin to invade antennal lobe at ~24 hr APF.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: PN dendrites and ORN axons match with their respective partners beginning at approximately 30 hr APF and establish discrete glomerular compartments at approximately 48 hr APF.
source: PN dendrites and ORN axons then match with their respective partners beginning at ~30 hr APF and establish discrete glomerular compartments at ~48 hr APF.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: After establishing discrete glomerular compartments, PNs expand their terminal branches, build synaptic connections, and finally form mature adult olfactory circuits.
source: Thereafter, they expand their terminal branches, build synaptic connections, and finally form mature adult olfactory circuits (Jefferis et al., 2004; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Jefferis et al., 2004) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The study performed scRNA-seq of PNs from four different developmental stages: 0–6 hr APF, 24–30 hr APF, 48–54 hr APF, and 1–5 days adult.
source: To better understand the molecular mechanisms that control these dynamic developmental processes underlying neural circuit assembly, we performed scRNA-seq of PNs from four different developmental stages: 0–6 hr APF, 24–30 hr APF, 48–54 hr APF, and 1–5 days adult (hereafter 0, 24, 48 hr APF and adult) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the experimental design.

claim: GH146-GAL4 was used to drive UAS-mCD8-GFP expression in most PNs at 24 hr, 48 hr, and adult stages.
source: We used ﻿GH146-GAL4 (Stocker et al., 1997) to drive UAS-mCD8-GFP (Lee and Luo, 1999) expression in most PNs at 24 hr, 48 hr, and adult, which labels ~90 of the estimated 150 PNs in each hemisphere, covering ~40 of the 50 PN types.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: GH146-GAL4 labels approximately 90 of the estimated 150 PNs in each hemisphere, covering approximately 40 of the 50 PN types.
source: We used ﻿GH146-GAL4 (Stocker et al., 1997) to drive UAS-mCD8-GFP (Lee and Luo, 1999) expression in most PNs at 24 hr, 48 hr, and adult, which labels ~90 of the estimated 150 PNs in each hemisphere, covering ~40 of the 50 PN types.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: At 0 hr APF, GH146-GAL4 also labels cells in the optic lobes.
source: At 0 hr APF, GH146-GAL4 also labels cells in the optic lobes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which are inseparable from the central brain by dissection.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VT033006-GAL4 was used to label PNs at 0 hr APF.
source: Therefore, we used VT033006-GAL4 to label PNs at 0 hr APF (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Tirian and Dickson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: VT033006-GAL4 labels most PNs from the anterodrosal and lateral lineage, but not PNs from the ventral lineage or anterior paired lateral (APL) neurons.
source: VT033006-GAL4 labels most PNs from the anterodrosal and lateral lineage, but not PNs from the ventral lineage or anterior paired lateral (APL) neurons like GH146-GAL4.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: VT033006-GAL4 is expressed in approximately 95 cells that innervate approximately 44 glomeruli which largely overlap with PNs labeled by GH146-GAL4.
source: It is expressed in ~95 cells that innervate ~44 glomeruli which largely overlap with PNs labeled by GH146-GAL4 (Inada et al., 2017; Elkahlah et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Inada et al., 2017; Elkahlah et al., 2020).

claim: The study obtained approximately 4900 high quality PNs for analysis.
source: On average ~3000 genes were detected per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and after quality filtering (see Materials and methods), we obtained ~3700 high quality PNs in addition to the previously sequenced ~1200 PNs (Li et al., 2017), yielding ~4900 PNs for analysis in this study (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the data obtained.

claim: All analyzed PNs express high levels of neuronal markers but not glial markers.
source: All analyzed PNs express high levels of neuronal markers but not glial markers, confirming the specificity of sequenced cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Unbiased clustering using overdispersed genes from all PNs readily separates them into different groups according to their stage.
source: Unbiased clustering using overdispersed genes from all PNs readily separates them into different groups according to their stage (Figure 1F), suggesting that gene expression changes across these four developmental stages represent a principal difference in their single-cell transcriptomes.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Gene expression changes across the four developmental stages represent a principal difference in PN single-cell transcriptomes.
source: Unbiased clustering using overdispersed genes from all PNs readily separates them into different groups according to their stage (Figure 1F), suggesting that gene expression changes across these four developmental stages represent a principal difference in their single-cell transcriptomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PNs cluster by developmental stage.

claim: PNs labeled by GH146-GAL4 at 24 hr APF form approximately 30 distinct transcriptomic clusters.
source: PNs labeled by GH146-GAL4 at 24 hr APF form ~30 distinct transcriptomic clusters.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and describes the data obtained.

claim: Six transcriptomic clusters were previously matched to specific anatomically and functionally defined PN types.
source: We previously matched six of these transcriptomic clusters to specific anatomically and functionally defined PN types (Li et al., 2017), hereafter referred to as 'decoding transcriptomic identity'.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2017).

claim: Unlike ORNs, whose identities can be decoded using uniquely expressed olfactory receptors, PNs lack known type-specific markers.
source: Unlike ORNs, whose identities can be decoded using uniquely expressed olfactory receptors (Li et al., 2020a), PNs lack known type-specific markers.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2020a).

claim: PN types are mostly specified by combinatorial expression of several genes.
source: Instead, PN types are mostly specified by combinatorial expression of several genes (Li et al., 2017), making it more challenging to decode their transcriptomic identities.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2017).

claim: split#28 GAL4 labeled two types of PNs—those that project their dendrites to the DC3 and DA4l glomeruli in developing and adult animals.
source: split#28 GAL4 labeled two types of PNs—those that project their dendrites to the DC3 and DA4l glomeruli in developing and adult animals (Figure 2A,B; note that PN types are named after the glomeruli they project their dendrites to).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2A,B.

claim: Split#28+ PNs fell into two distinct clusters when visualized using tSNE.
source: Split#28+ PNs (orange dots) fell into two distinct clusters and intermingled with GH146+ PNs (gray dots) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2C.

claim: One cluster of split#28+ PNs mapped to previously decoded DC3 PNs.
source: One cluster mapped to previously decoded DC3 PNs (Li et al., 2017), and the other cluster expressed zfh2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2017) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The other cluster of split#28+ PNs expressed zfh2 and represents DA4l PNs.
source: One cluster mapped to previously decoded DC3 PNs (Li et al., 2017), and the other cluster expressed zfh2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). We validated that this cluster indeed represents DA4l PNs by visualizing the expression of zfh2 in PNs utilizing an intersectional strategy by combining zfh2-GAL4, GH146-Flp, and UAS-FRT-STOP-FRT-mCD8-GFP (hereafter referred to as 'intersecting with GH146-Flp') (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: split#7 GAL4 labeled three types of PNs in the adult stage.
source: split#7 GAL4 labeled three types of PNs in the adult stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: When split#7 GAL4 labeled cells were sequenced at 24 hr APF and visualized using tSNE, eight distinct clusters were found.
source: However, when we sequenced cells labeled by this GAL4 line at 24 hr APF and visualized them using tSNE, we found eight distinct clusters (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2F.

claim: The discrepancy between the number of PN types labeled by split#7 GAL4 in adults versus at 24 hr APF is due to loss of driver expression in adult stage for some PN types.
source: We reasoned that this could be due to loss of driver expression in adult stage for some PN types.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that more clusters are found at 24 hr APF than in adults.

claim: Using a permanent labeling strategy, split#7 GAL4 was observed to label eight types of PNs.
source: To test this hypothesis and reveal PNs that are labeled by this driver transiently during development, we used a permanent labeling strategy to label all cells that express split#7 GAL4 at any time of development (split#7+ PNs hereafter) by combining it with UAS-mCD8-GFP, Actin promoter-FRT-STOP-FRT-GAL4, and UAS-Flp. Using this strategy, we observed labeling of eight types of PNs (Figure 2D), consistent with number of clusters we observed by sequencing.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Among split#7+ PNs, four types belong to the adPN lineage (acj6+) and the other four types belong to the lPN lineage (vvl+).
source: Among split#7+ PNs, four types belong to the adPN lineage (acj6+) and the other four types belong to the lPN lineage (vvl+) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2E.

claim: By intersecting GAL4 lines with GH146-Flp, all seven previously unknown transcriptomic clusters among split#7+ PNs were mapped to seven PN types.
source: We identified differentially expressed genes among split#7+ PNs and obtained existing GAL4 lines mimicking their expression. By intersecting those GAL4 lines with GH146-Flp, we mapped all seven previously unknown transcriptomic clusters to seven PN types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H; see legends for detailed description).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H.

claim: The gene knot (kn) was expressed in seven transcriptomic clusters among all GH146+ PNs.
source: One such marker was the gene knot (kn), which was expressed in seven transcriptomic clusters among all GH146+ PNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: When kn-GAL4 was intersected with GH146-Flp, six types of adPNs (acj6+) and several vPNs (Lim1+) were labeled.
source: When kn-GAL4 was intersected with GH146-Flp, six types of adPNs (acj6+) and several vPNs (Lim1+) were labeled (Figure 2G,J).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2G,J.

claim: GH146-Flp is expressed in VM5v PNs at some point during development.
source: Although it has been previously reported that GH146-GAL4 is not expressed in VM5v PNs (Yu et al., 2010), labeling of these PNs when GH146-Flp was intersected with either kn-GAL4 or split#15 GAL4 indicates that GH146-Flp must be expressed in VM5v PNs at some point during development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that VM5v PNs are labeled when GH146-Flp is intersected with other GAL4 lines, despite prior reports that GH146-GAL4 is not expressed in VM5v PNs.

claim: DIP-beta is expressed in one kn+ vPN cluster but not in lPNs innervating DA1 glomerulus.
source: We found that DIP-beta was expressed in one kn+ vPN cluster but not in lPNs innervating DA1 glomerulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3F,G.

claim: Intersecting DIP-beta-GAL4 with GH146-Flp confirmed that DIP-beta+ vPN targeted their dendrites to DA1 glomerulus.
source: Intersecting DIP-beta-GAL4 with GH146-Flp confirmed that DIP-beta+ vPN indeed targeted their dendrites to DA1 glomerulus, illustrating the DIP-beta+ vPN cluster to be DA1 vPNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3H.

claim: A total of 21 transcriptomic clusters corresponding to anatomically defined PN types at 24 hr APF have been mapped.
source: In summary, by sequencing a small number of known PN types at a time and analyzing the expression pattern of differentially expressed genes, we have now mapped a total of 21 transcriptomic clusters corresponding to anatomically defined PN types at 24 hr APF (Figure 2K,L).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 2K,L.

claim: All sequenced PNs segregated into different clusters according to their developmental stages using unbiased, over-dispersed genes for clustering regardless of PN types.
source: All sequenced PNs segregated into different clusters according to their developmental stages using unbiased, over-dispersed genes for clustering regardless of PN types (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 1F.

claim: Even when using genes identified by ICIM for clustering, individual PNs were separated principally by developmental stages.
source: Even when we used the genes identified by ICIM for clustering, which emphasizes the differences between different PN types (Li et al., 2017), we still observed that individual PNs were separated principally by developmental stages (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 3A and a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2017).

claim: Neural development-related genes, including those with functions in morphogenesis and cytoskeleton organization, were enriched in developing PNs.
source: Consistent with our previous knowledge, neural development-related genes, including those with functions in morphogenesis and cytoskeleton organization, were enriched in developing PNs (Figure 3C, D); genes related to synaptic transmission, ion transport, and behavior, on the other hand, were upregulated in mature PNs (Figure 3C, E; Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 3C,D and citations to prior literature (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020b).

claim: Genes related to synaptic transmission, ion transport, and behavior were upregulated in mature PNs.
source: Consistent with our previous knowledge, neural development-related genes, including those with functions in morphogenesis and cytoskeleton organization, were enriched in developing PNs (Figure 3C, D); genes related to synaptic transmission, ion transport, and behavior, on the other hand, were upregulated in mature PNs (Figure 3C, E; Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 3C,E and citations to prior literature (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020b).

claim: At 0 hr APF, PNs always formed two distinct clusters—a larger cluster consisting of both adPNs and lPNs, and a smaller one with only adPNs.
source: At 0 hr APF, PNs always formed two distinct clusters—a larger cluster consisting of both adPNs and lPNs, and a smaller one with only adPNs (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The smaller cluster at 0 hr APF represents embryonically born PNs, which undergo axon and dendrite pruning during early metamorphosis.
source: We hypothesized that the smaller cluster could represent embryonically born PNs, which undergo axon and dendrite pruning during early metamorphosis (Marin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis stated in the Results section and is supported by a citation to prior literature (Marin et al., 2005).

claim: Sox14, Mical, Cullin1, and two ESCRT genes—shrb and Vps20—showed higher expression levels in the smaller cluster at 0 hr APF.
source: We found that Sox14, Mical, Cullin1, and two sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) genes—shrb and Vps20, indeed showed higher expression levels in the smaller cluster (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Two types of embryonically born PNs, DA4l and VA6 PNs, were mapped to the smaller cluster at 0 hr APF.
source: We also confirmed our hypothesis by mapping two types of embryonically born PNs, DA4l and VA6 PNs, to this smaller cluster (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B; see mapping details in Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Figure 7.

claim: At 24 hr APF, the highest number of clusters reflecting different PN types was observed.
source: At 24 hr APF, we observed the highest number of clusters reflecting different PN types.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Quantifications of transcriptomic similarity among PNs at each stage confirmed the highest diversity among PNs at 24 hr APF.
source: Quantifications of transcriptomic similarity among PNs at each stage indeed confirmed the highest diversity among PNs at 24 hr APF (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 4E–G.

claim: At 24 hr APF, PNs refine their dendrites to specific regions and begin to prepare themselves as targets for their partner ORN axons.
source: This is likely explained by the fact that at this stage, PNs refine their dendrites to specific regions and begin to prepare themselves as targets for their partner ORN axons.
evidence: This claim is stated as an explanation for the observed high transcriptomic diversity at 24 hr APF.

claim: PN axons at the lateral horn begin to establish their characteristic branching patterns at 24 hr APF.
source: In addition, PN axons at the lateral horn begin to establish their characteristic branching patterns (Jefferis et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Jefferis et al., 2004).

claim: Adult PNs only formed three clusters representing cholinergic excitatory PNs and two Gad1+ GABAergic inhibitory cell types—vPNs and APL neurons.
source: In contrast to the high transcriptomic diversity in 24 hr APF PNs, adult PNs only formed three clusters (Figure 4A bottom, indicated by dashed lines). The three clusters represent cholinergic excitatory PNs (marked by VAChT), and two Gad1+ GABAergic inhibitory cell types—vPNs and APL neurons (VGlut+), respectively (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 4A and Figure 4H.

claim: After wiring specificity is achieved, all excitatory PNs may perform similar functions, but distinct from inhibitory neuronal types.
source: This is likely because after wiring specificity is achieved, all excitatory PNs may perform similar functions, but distinct from inhibitory neuronal types.
evidence: This claim is stated as an explanation for the observed low transcriptomic diversity in adult PNs.

claim: At different developmental stages, the differentially expressed genes identified all revealed the most defining biological processes those neurons are undertaking.
source: Thus, at different developmental stages, the differentially expressed genes we identified all revealed the most defining biological processes those neurons are undertaking.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented.

claim: PN transcriptomes reflect the pruning process of embryonically born PNs at 0 hr APF.
source: Our observations showed that PN transcriptomes reflect the pruning process of embryonically born PNs at 0 hr APF, PN type and wiring distinction at 24 hr APF, and neurotransmitter type in adults.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented.

claim: PN transcriptomes reflect PN type and wiring distinction at 24 hr APF.
source: Our observations showed that PN transcriptomes reflect the pruning process of embryonically born PNs at 0 hr APF, PN type and wiring distinction at 24 hr APF, and neurotransmitter type in adults.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented.

claim: PN transcriptomes reflect neurotransmitter type in adults.
source: Our observations showed that PN transcriptomes reflect the pruning process of embryonically born PNs at 0 hr APF, PN type and wiring distinction at 24 hr APF, and neurotransmitter type in adults.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented.

claim: The gene set identified by ICIM from 24 hr APF PNs outperformed all other gene sets in separating different PN types at all timepoints.
source: We found that this gene set outperformed all other gene sets in separating different PN types at all timepoints (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Most gene sets found by different methods at 24 hr APF exceeded gene sets identified at other stages for clustering PNs according to their types.
source: In fact, most gene sets found by different methods at 24 hr APF, including overdispersed genes, ICIM genes, as well as differentially expressed genes between different clusters, exceeded gene sets identified at other stages for clustering PNs according to their types (data not shown), further confirming that transcriptomes of 24 hr APF PNs carry the most information for distinguishing different PN types, even for other developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Transcriptomes of 24 hr APF PNs carry the most information for distinguishing different PN types, even for other developmental stages.
source: In fact, most gene sets found by different methods at 24 hr APF, including overdispersed genes, ICIM genes, as well as differentially expressed genes between different clusters, exceeded gene sets identified at other stages for clustering PNs according to their types (data not shown), further confirming that transcriptomes of 24 hr APF PNs carry the most information for distinguishing different PN types, even for other developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: MARS was applied to identify and annotate cell types using 24 hr APF as the starting annotated dataset.
source: We applied meta-learned representations for single-cell data (MARS) for identifying and annotating cell types (Brbić et al., 2020). MARS learns to project cells using deep neural networks in the latent low-dimensional space in which cells group according to their cell types. We used 24 hr APF, the stage with highest transcriptome diversity, as the starting annotated dataset to learn shared low-dimensional space for 48 hr APF, 0 hr APF, and eventually the adult dataset.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by a citation to prior literature (Brbić et al., 2020).

claim: Using MARS, approximately 30 cell types were found in each stage.
source: Using this approach, we found ~30 cell types in each stage (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 5B.

claim: MARS cluster annotations were validated using two distinct methods: HDBSCAN clustering based on tSNEs and Leiden clustering based on neighborhood graphs.
source: Independently, we also validated MARS cluster annotations using two distinct methods: HDBSCAN clustering based on tSNEs and Leiden clustering based on neighborhood graphs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Blondel et al., 2008; Levine et al., 2015; Traag et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature (Blondel et al., 2008; Levine et al., 2015; Traag et al., 2019).

claim: MARS performed better at segregating some closely related clusters representing multiple PN types compared to HDBSCAN and Leiden methods.
source: We compared cluster annotations by these three methods to known PN types at 24 hr APF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) and found that even at this stage, MARS performed better at segregating some closely related clusters representing multiple PN types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: At 0 hr APF and the adult stage, MARS identified more clusters compared to the other methods.
source: At 0 hr APF and the adult stage, MARS identified more clusters compared to the other methods, demonstrating the robustness of MARS at identifying unique cell types.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Batch correction methods including Harmony, BBKNN, ComBat, and Scanorama were attempted but did not reliably match transcriptomes of same PN types across different developmental stages.
source: We first tried to apply some batch correction methods, including Harmony, BBKNN, ComBat, and Scanorama, to our dataset to correct for the transcriptomic changes of PNs throughout development (Hie et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2007; Korsunsky et al., 2019; Polański et al., 2020). For all batch correction methods attempted, we observed instances of (1) PNs of the same type at the same stage split into different clusters; (2) PNs of different types merge into the same cluster; (3) no distinguishable cluster formation for many PNs in stages other than 24 hr APF.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by citations to prior literature (Hie et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2007; Korsunsky et al., 2019; Polański et al., 2020).

claim: The study collected PNs labeled by kn-GAL4 from 24 hr APF, 48 hr APF, and adult brains for scRNA-seq as a test case for matching PN types across stages.
source: To perform this task, we first used kn+ PNs as test case. We collected PNs labeled by kn-GAL4 from 24 hr APF, 48 hr APF, and adult brains for scRNA-seq (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Dimensionality reduction of kn+ PNs showed a consistent number of clusters across stages, with one exception of an extra vPN cluster observed at 48 hr APF and adult stages.
source: Dimensionality reduction of these cells showed a consistent number of clusters across stages (Figure 6B). One exception is an extra vPN cluster observed at 48 hr APF and adult stages. This discrepancy with 24 hr APF data is likely caused by the lower number of vPNs sequenced at 24 hr APF.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Using the two approaches, all kn+ PN types (six adPNs and three vPNs) were matched from three different stages.
source: Using these two approaches, we were able to match the same types of PNs across three developmental stages, and the results from the two approaches consistently agreed with each other (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 6G.

claim: As development proceeds from 24 hr APF and 48 hr APF to adults, the transcriptomic difference between identified PN types becomes smaller.
source: In addition, these data further validated an earlier conclusion (Figure 4) that as development proceeds from 24 hr APF and 48 hr APF to adults, the transcriptomic difference between identified PN types becomes smaller (Figure 6G; quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Using both manual and automatic approaches, many PN types were matched across two or more developmental stages, including 18 PN types that were decoded and seven transcriptomic clusters with unknown identity.
source: Using both manual and automatic approaches, we were able to match many PN types across two or more developmental stages (Figure 7B), which includes 18 PN types that we have decoded in Figure 2 as well as seven transcriptomic clusters with unknown identity.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 7B.

claim: The majority of the PNs matched were confirmed by both the automatic (transcriptomic similarity-based) and manual (marker-based) methods.
source: The majority of the PNs we matched were confirmed by both the automatic (transcriptomic similarity-based) and manual (marker-based) methods (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Hierarchical clustering on all excitatory PN clusters showed some lineage-related similarity between PN types at 0 hr APF.
source: We observed some lineage-related similarity between PN types at 0 hr APF: transcriptomes of PNs from the same lineage tended to be clustered together in the dendrogram and their correlations are higher, although the relationship was not absolute.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Lineage-related similarity between PN types was gradually lost as development proceeded.
source: Such similarity was gradually lost as development proceeded (as inferred by both the dendrogram as well as correlation between PNs from the same lineage).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: 0 hr and 24 hr APF PNs exhibited high correlations between their birth orders and transcriptomic similarities.
source: The results confirmed that 0 hr and 24 hr APF PNs, but not 48 hr APF and adult PNs, exhibited high correlations between their birth orders and transcriptomic similarities.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by permutation tests.

claim: 48 hr APF and adult PNs did not exhibit high correlations between their birth orders and transcriptomic similarities.
source: The results confirmed that 0 hr and 24 hr APF PNs, but not 48 hr APF and adult PNs, exhibited high correlations between their birth orders and transcriptomic similarities.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by permutation tests.

claim: Developmental trajectory analysis of adPNs born at the larval stage using Monocle 3 showed that the unbiased pseudo time recapitulated their birth order.
source: In addition, developmental trajectory analysis of adPNs born at the larval stage using Monocle 3 (Cao et al., 2019) also showed that the unbiased pseudo time recapitulated their birth order (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 8D and a citation to prior literature (Cao et al., 2019).

claim: A previous study profiled the transcriptomes of PN neuroblasts at various larval stages and identified 63 genes with temporal gradients.
source: A previous study profiled the transcriptomes of PN neuroblasts at various larval stages and identified 63 genes with temporal gradients (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Liu et al., 2015).

claim: Two RNA-binding proteins, Imp and Syp, regulate the fate of PNs born at different times.
source: Among those genes, the authors have validated that two RNA-binding proteins, Imp and Syp, regulate the fate of PNs born at different times.
evidence: This claim is stated as a finding from a previous study.

claim: 15 out of the 63 genes with temporal gradients in PN neuroblasts (including Imp but not Syp) maintained some temporal gradient patterns according to their birth order at 0 hr APF but not at later stages.
source: We found 15 out of the 63 genes (including Imp but not Syp) maintained some temporal gradient patterns according to their birth order at 0 hr APF (Figure 8E) but not at the later stages (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 8E.

claim: The expression of a subset of birth order-related genes in adPN neuroblast, including a cell-fate regulator, is maintained in postmitotic PNs till early pupal stage.
source: This result suggested that the expression of a subset of birth order-related genes in adPN neuroblast, including a cell-fate regulator, is maintained in postmitotic PNs till early pupal stage.
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation of the data in the Results section.

claim: PN types with adjacent birth order shared more similar transcriptomes, reflecting temporal gene expression dynamics of their progenitor.
source: In summary, our data demonstrated that PN types with adjacent birth order shared more similar transcriptomes, reflecting temporal gene expression dynamics of their progenitor.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented.

claim: Transcriptomic similarity between PN types with adjacent birth order was maintained at early pupal stages and was gradually lost as PNs mature.
source: Such transcriptomic similarity was maintained at early pupal stages and was gradually lost as PNs mature.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement in the Results section based on the data presented.

claim: The similarities between different PN types are not fixed across development.
source: Hierarchical clustering on the principal components calculated using the entire gene matrix indicates that the similarities between different PN types are not fixed across development (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The differentially expressed genes in PNs differ across developmental stages.
source: This suggests that the differentially expressed genes in PNs differ across developmental stages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that similarities between PN types change across development.

claim: Around 500 differentially expressed genes were found at 24 hr APF, 48 hr APF, and the adult stage.
source: Using this criterion, we found around 500 DE genes at 24 hr APF, 48 hr APF, and the adult stage (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9A.

claim: At 0 hr APF, many more differentially expressed genes were identified, mostly contributed by the embryonically born PNs.
source: At 0 hr APF, many more DE genes were identified. The larger gene set at this stage is mostly contributed by the embryonically born PNs (1015 out of 1393 genes), which have transcriptomically distinct features because these neurons undergo axon and dendrite pruning (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 4A–D.

claim: 103 genes were differentially expressed throughout development, 52 of which were differentially expressed among the 12 PN types matched across all four stages.
source: We intersected the four lists of DE genes to find genes that are differentially expressed throughout development. This resulted in 103 genes, 52 of which were differentially expressed among the 12 PN types we matched across all four stages.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Among the differentially expressed genes that are differentially expressed in all four stages, there is an over-representation of transcription factors (TFs) and cell surface molecules (CSMs) compared to their genome-wide fractions.
source: Among the DE genes that are differentially expressed in all four stages, we observed an over-representation of transcription factors (TFs) and cell surface molecules (CSMs) compared to their genome-wide fractions (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9B.

claim: Genes in the transcription factor and cell surface molecule categories play critical roles in PN wiring.
source: Previous studies have shown that genes in these two categories play critical roles in PN wiring (Hong and Luo, 2014; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Hong and Luo, 2014; Li et al., 2017).

claim: The majority of transcription factors are expressed in both lineages, while a small fraction of TFs is lineage-specific.
source: While the majority of TFs are expressed in both lineages, expression of a small fraction of TFs is lineage-specific.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Expression of acj6, kn, C15, and salr is limited to PNs from the anterodorsal lineage.
source: For example, expression of acj6, kn, C15, and salr is limited to PNs from the anterodorsal lineage, whereas vvl and unpg are only expressed in PNs from the lateral lineage (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: vvl and unpg are only expressed in PNs from the lateral lineage.
source: For example, expression of acj6, kn, C15, and salr is limited to PNs from the anterodorsal lineage, whereas vvl and unpg are only expressed in PNs from the lateral lineage (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transcription factors are generally expressed in a binary fashion throughout development.
source: Furthermore, although TFs are generally expressed in a binary fashion throughout development (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), many CSMs exhibit graded expression with complex temporal dynamics (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many cell surface molecules exhibit graded expression with complex temporal dynamics.
source: Furthermore, although TFs are generally expressed in a binary fashion throughout development (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), many CSMs exhibit graded expression with complex temporal dynamics (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observation that many CSMs exhibit graded expression with complex temporal dynamics is consistent with observations made from single-cell transcriptome studies in the developing Drosophila optic lobe.
source: This is consistent with observations made from single-cell transcriptome studies in the developing Drosophila optic lobe (Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020; Özel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020; Özel et al., 2021).

claim: Among the CSMs that are differentially expressed in any of the four stages, many molecules in protein families that have been implicated in wiring were observed, including Beaten Path (Beat), Dpr, DIP, Dscam, Fasciclin (Fas), and Robo.
source: Among the CSMs that are differentially expressed in any of the four stages, we observed many molecules in protein families that have been implicated in wiring, including Beaten Path (Beat), Dpr, DIP, Dscam, ﻿Fasciclin (Fas), and Robo (Figure 9—figure supplement 2; Kolodkin and Tessier-Lavigne, 2011; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior literature (Kolodkin and Tessier-Lavigne, 2011; Sanes and Zipursky, 2020).

claim: The differentially expressed gene list may contain an enriched set of wiring-related molecules.
source: Thus, this differentially expressed gene list may contain an enriched set of wiring-related molecules, some of which have been studied in the context of wiring.
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation of the data in the Results section.

claim: Some genes with differential expression pattern at the protein level, such as Ten-a and Ten-m, do not exhibit obvious differential expression at the mRNA level.
source: On the other hand, we note that some genes with differential expression pattern at the protein level, such as Ten-a and Ten-m (Hong et al., 2012), do not exhibit obvious differential expression at the mRNA level.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by a citation to prior literature (Hong et al., 2012).

claim: The observation that some genes with differential expression at the protein level do not exhibit differential expression at the mRNA level highlights the existence of post-transcriptional regulation for some genes that are not captured by transcriptomic analysis.
source: This highlighted the existence of post-transcriptional regulation for some genes that are not captured by transcriptomic analysis.
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation of the data in the Results section.

claim: More than a third of the differentially expressed genes were shared between 24 hr APF and adult stages.
source: We found that more than a third of the DE genes were shared between these two stages (Figure 10A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 10A.

claim: Shared differentially expressed genes between 24 hr APF and adult stages were predominately related to neural development.
source: Gene Ontology analysis revealed that these shared genes were predominately related to neural development (Figure 10B, middle).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 10B.

claim: Some differentially expressed genes found among adult PN types were developmentally differentially expressed genes, some of which could play a role in the maintenance of adult nervous system structures.
source: These data suggested that some DE genes found among adult PN types were developmentally differentially expressed genes, some of which could play a role in the maintenance of adult nervous system structures.
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation of the data in the Results section.

claim: Many Gene Ontology terms related to the physiological properties of PNs were observed among the adult-only differentially expressed genes.
source: Interestingly, many Gene Ontology terms related to the physiological properties of PNs were observed among the adult-only DE genes (Figure 10B, bottom).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 10B.

claim: Several adult differentially expressed genes belong to the ion channels or transmembrane receptor gene groups.
source: Indeed, several adult DE genes belong to the ion channels or transmembrane receptor (including neurotransmitter receptors and G-protein-coupled receptors) gene groups (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Results section and is supported by reference to Figure 10C.

claim: PN types in adults acquire new categories of differentially expressed genes, and those genes might lead to differences in the physiological properties between different PN types.
source: These results demonstrated that PN types in adults acquire new categories of differentially expressed genes, and those genes might lead to differences in the physiological properties between different PN types.
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation of the data in the Results section.

claim: Cell-type classification based on single-cell transcriptomes largely agrees with classifications by more traditional criteria such as morphology, physiology, connectivity, and signature molecular markers.
source: Many studies have illustrated that cell-type classification based on the single-cell transcriptomes largely agrees with classifications by some of the more traditional criteria (Zeng and Sanes, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Zeng and Sanes, 2017).

claim: For Drosophila olfactory PNs, the most prominent type-specific feature is their pre- and post-synaptic connections.
source: For Drosophila olfactory PNs, the most prominent type-specific feature is their pre- and post-synaptic connections, which determines their olfactory response profiles and the higher order neurons they relay olfactory information to.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: Different PN types are largely defined by the differences in their connectivity.
source: Thus, different PN types are largely defined by the differences in their connectivity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: The transcriptomic identity of PNs corresponds well with their types during development.
source: We have previously observed that the transcriptomic identity of PNs corresponds well with their types during development, and for three identified PN types, transcriptomic differences peak during the circuit assembly stage (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2017).

claim: For three identified PN types, transcriptomic differences peak during the circuit assembly stage.
source: We have previously observed that the transcriptomic identity of PNs corresponds well with their types during development, and for three identified PN types, transcriptomic differences peak during the circuit assembly stage (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Li et al., 2017).

claim: The study generalized the finding that transcriptomic differences peak during circuit assembly across many more PN types by showing that transcriptomic differences are the highest around 24 hr APF.
source: Here, we generalized these findings across many more PN types by showing that transcriptomic differences are the highest around 24 hr APF, a stage when PNs are making wiring decisions and preparing cues for subsequent ORN–PN matching (Figure 4), and by demonstrating that clustering of PNs according to their types from all stages are best done using differentially expressed genes at 24 hr APF (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by reference to Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: Clustering of PNs according to their types from all stages are best done using differentially expressed genes at 24 hr APF.
source: Here, we generalized these findings across many more PN types by showing that transcriptomic differences are the highest around 24 hr APF, a stage when PNs are making wiring decisions and preparing cues for subsequent ORN–PN matching (Figure 4), and by demonstrating that clustering of PNs according to their types from all stages are best done using differentially expressed genes at 24 hr APF (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by reference to Figure 5.

claim: At certain stages, differences among type-specific genes can be masked by other genes belonging to pathways of a more dominating biological process.
source: Additionally, our data indicate that at certain stages, differences among those type-specific genes can be masked by other genes belonging to pathways of a more dominating biological process (such as neurite pruning at 0 hr APF for PNs).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: It may be challenging to identify genes carrying type-specific information at certain timepoints even when sophisticated algorithms are applied, which can lead to underestimation of cell type diversity.
source: As a consequence, it may be challenging to identify genes carrying type-specific information at certain timepoints even when sophisticated algorithms are applied, which can lead to underestimation of cell type diversity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The observation of peaked transcriptome diversity in developing PNs has also been observed in the Drosophila optic lobe recently.
source: Our observation of peaked transcriptome diversity in developing PNs has also been observed in the Drosophila optic lobe recently (Özel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Özel et al., 2021).

claim: In order to accurately classify single-cell transcriptomes, especially for connectivity-defined neuronal types such as fly olfactory PNs, it may be a general strategy to first obtain their single-cell transcriptomes during circuit assembly and then use this information to supervise cell-type classification in other developmental stages, including adults.
source: Thus, in order to accurately classify single-cell transcriptomes, especially for connectivity-defined neuronal types such as fly olfactory PNs, it may be a general strategy to first obtain their single-cell transcriptomes during circuit assembly and then use this information to supervise cell-type classification in other developmental stages, including adults.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed general strategy based on the findings.

claim: Both cell types and their biological states can split single-cell transcriptomes into distinct clusters.
source: Both cell types and their biological states can split single-cell transcriptomes into distinct clusters (Zeng and Sanes, 2017; Cembrowski and Menon, 2018; Tasic, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Zeng and Sanes, 2017; Cembrowski and Menon, 2018; Tasic, 2018).

claim: The same PN types of different developmental stages—reflecting different states—exhibit very distinct transcriptomic profiles.
source: We observed that the same PN types of different developmental stages—reflecting different states—indeed exhibit very distinct transcriptomic profiles (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by reference to Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The study developed and applied two complementary methods—one manual based on marker gene expression, and one automatic based on similarity between transcriptomic clusters—to identify transcriptomic clusters corresponding to the same PN types across multiple timepoints.
source: To identify transcriptomic clusters corresponding to the same PN types across multiple timepoints, we developed and applied two complementary methods—one manual based on the marker gene expression, and one automatic based on the similarity between transcriptomic clusters.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the methodological approach.

claim: By applying both methods, the study can confidently track the transcriptomes of the same cell type throughout development and study the unique molecular features of each stage.
source: By applying both methods, we can confidently track the transcriptomes of the same cell type throughout development and study the unique molecular features of each stage.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the methodological approach.

claim: Two other methods for tracing transcriptomes of the same neuronal types across development—batch-correction to cluster same cell types across different stages, and training an artificial neural network to classify cell type—have been applied successfully in recent single-cell transcriptome studies of cells in the developing Drosophila optic lobe.
source: We note that two other methods for tracing transcriptomes of the same neuronal types across development—batch-correction to cluster same cell types across different stages, and training an artificial neural network to classify cell type—have been applied successfully in recent single-cell transcriptome studies of cells in the developing Drosophila optic lobe (Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020; Özel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020; Özel et al., 2021).

claim: The methods developed in this study can be applied to other single-cell studies where diverse cell types and multiple states are involved.
source: Together, those methods can be applied to other single-cell studies where diverse cell types and multiple states are involved.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed application of the methods.

claim: The methods developed in this study can be especially useful for tissues with high cellular diversity but lack unique markers for each cell type.
source: Those methods can be especially useful for tissues with high cellular diversity but lack unique markers for each cell type.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed application of the methods.

claim: The study obtained high-quality single-cell transcriptomes of most excitatory PNs from early pupal stage to adulthood.
source: In this study, we have obtained high-quality single-cell transcriptomes of most excitatory PNs from early pupal stage to adulthood (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: The study used combinations of markers and drivers to decode the transcriptomic identity of 21 transcriptomic clusters at 24 hr APF.
source: We have used combinations of markers and drivers to decode the transcriptomic identity of 21 transcriptomic clusters at 24 hr APF (Figure 2), and matched clusters representing the same PN type across four developmental stages (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: The study matched clusters representing the same PN type across four developmental stages.
source: We have used combinations of markers and drivers to decode the transcriptomic identity of 21 transcriptomic clusters at 24 hr APF (Figure 2), and matched clusters representing the same PN type across four developmental stages (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by reference to Figure 7.

claim: Using the rich and well-annotated dataset, researchers can now explore different aspects of PN development and function to identify candidate molecules for future studies.
source: Using this rich and well-annotated dataset, researchers can now explore different aspects of PN development and function to identify candidate molecules for future studies.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed use of the data.

claim: One can search for novel molecules involved in neurite pruning among the differentially expressed genes between the embryonically-born and larval-born PNs at 0 hr APF.
source: For example, one can search for novel molecules involved in neurite pruning among the differentially expressed genes between the embryonically-born and larval-born PNs at 0 hr APF (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed use of the data and is supported by reference to Figure 4B–D.

claim: Developmentally enriched genes and genes that are differentially expressed among different PN types can be good candidates for studies on neural development and wiring specificity.
source: Developmentally enriched genes and genes that are differentially expressed among different PN types, on the other hand, can be good candidates for studies on neural development and wiring specificity (Figure 3 and Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed use of the data and is supported by reference to Figure 3 and Figure 9.

claim: Differentially expressed neuronal signaling genes in adult PNs can be used to explore differences in physiological properties and information processing.
source: Differentially expressed neuronal signaling genes in adult PNs can be used to explore differences in physiological properties and information processing (Figure 10).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed use of the data and is supported by reference to Figure 10.

claim: Driver lines for specific types of PNs can be made using genes that show consistent expression pattern across different stages to label and genetically manipulate specific PN types.
source: In addition, driver lines for specific types of PNs can be made using genes that show consistent expression pattern across different stages (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) to label and genetically manipulate specific PN types.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed use of the data and is supported by reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Together with several recent in depth scRNAseq studies of cells in the visual and olfactory system across multiple stages, these studies have established foundations of gene expression for Drosophila olfactory and visual systems and should catalyze new biological discoveries.
source: Together with several recent in depth scRNAseq studies of cells in the visual and olfactory system across multiple stages (Jain et al., 2020; Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020; McLaughlin et al., 2021; Özel et al., 2021), these studies have established foundations of gene expression for Drosophila olfactory and visual systems and should catalyze new biological discoveries.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citations to prior literature (Jain et al., 2020; Kurmangaliyev et al., 2020; McLaughlin et al., 2021; Özel et al., 2021).
